## Natural history notes

A native evergreen small tree or large shrub in the laurel family, characterized by aromatic leaves with densely hairy, reddish-brown undersides, small pale flowers, and dark blue to black berry-like fruits. Swamp Redbay occurs throughout Florida in wet forests and wetlands, including swamps, bayheads, pocosins, coastal swales, and other sites with moist, often peaty soils. It is especially well adapted to poorly drained conditions and can be distinguished from Redbay by its more densely hairy leaves and preference for wetter habitats. Its fruits are eaten by birds and other wildlife, while the foliage supports several insects. Like other native laurels, it is highly susceptible to laurel wilt disease spread by the non-native redbay ambrosia beetle.
